nameStory: The 'speedwell' name comes from an old English farewell blessing meaning 'God speed you well' or 'may you prosper.' These little flowers were thought to bring good luck to travelers. The 'alpine' part tells us exactly where this tough little plant makes its home - high up in the mountains where few other flowers dare to grow.
description: American alpine speedwell is a small, low-growing perennial wildflower that hugs the ground in high mountain areas. This hardy little plant rarely grows taller than 6 inches and spreads along the ground with creeping stems. Its tiny blue or purple flowers peek up from oval leaves, creating delicate splashes of color in harsh mountain environments. Despite its small size, this speedwell is incredibly tough, surviving freezing temperatures and intense mountain weather.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny blue to purple flowers with four rounded petals, each about the size of a pencil eraser, growing singly or in small clusters from the leaf joints - they feel papery when touched

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, feeling slightly fuzzy and thick to the touch, often with a slightly waxy surface that helps them retain moisture

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing mat-forming plant that creeps along the ground with trailing stems, rarely exceeding 6 inches in height but spreading outward in patches

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small heart-shaped seed capsules that split open when ripe, releasing tiny seeds that rattle softly when the dried capsule is shaken

habitat: In New England, this rare alpine plant is found only on the highest mountain peaks, particularly in the White Mountains of New Hampshire and possibly the highest elevations of Vermont's Green Mountains. It grows in moist, rocky areas above treeline, often tucked into crevices between boulders or in thin soils near snowfields. Look for it in areas where mountain avens, diapensia, and other true alpine plants grow.

seasonality.spring: Emerges from snow cover late in the season as alpine areas slowly warm, with new growth appearing as small green patches against dark rock.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from mid to late summer when most mountain snow has melted, producing its tiny blue flowers that may continue into early fall in favorable conditions.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, with the plant beginning to prepare for the long mountain winter by storing energy in its roots.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant under deep snow cover, with only the root system surviving the harsh alpine winter conditions.

funFact: This little speedwell is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only 9 times by naturalists - making it one of the most elusive wildflowers in the region, yet it thrives across the Arctic from Alaska to Greenland where it's much more common!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small blue alpine flowers like alpine forget-me-nots, but speedwells have four-petaled flowers (not five like forget-me-nots) and heart-shaped seed pods. Remember: 'Four for speedwell, five for forget-me-not.'
contextualKnowledge: This plant is named after Danish botanist Morten Wormskjold, who collected Arctic plants in Greenland in the early 1800s with help from local Greenlandic people. The rarity in New England reflects that we're at the southern edge of its range - it's much more at home in true Arctic conditions.
compareHints: Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family. While heath speedwell and thyme-leaved speedwell form loose mats in lower elevations, this species creates tight, compact growth to survive alpine winds. Its flowers are also smaller and more intensely colored than most other New England speedwells.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
